title: First Letter Seen Only Once
statement:
You get a string s of lowercase letters. Find the first position whose letter appears exactly once in the whole string and return that index (0-based).

If every letter appears at least twice, return -1.

examples.why: "s" appears three times. "w" at index 1 appears once. "i" also appears once, but it comes later.
Both "n" and "o" appear twice, so no letter is unique.
"a" and "b" look alone next to their neighbours but repeat further on. Only the whole-string count matters.

constraints: s contains only lowercase English letters
hints: Whether a letter is unique depends on the whole string, not on the letters around it. What do you need to know before you can decide about the first letter?
Count every letter first. A second pass can then ask a simple question at each position.
Pass one fills a count table of 26 slots. Pass two returns the first index whose letter has count 1.

explain.intuition:
You cannot decide about position 0 until you have seen the rest of the string, because its twin might be the very last letter. So split the work in two: first count how often each letter occurs, then walk the string again in order and stop at the first letter whose count is 1.

With only 26 possible letters, the count table is a fixed-size array, so the extra memory is constant. It is the same move as counting tag names in a DOM before deciding which ones are unique.
steps: For each letter in s, increase its slot.
Walk s again from index 0. Return the first index i where count[s[i]] === 1.
pitfalls: Comparing a letter only with its neighbours. In "abcba" the first a has no equal neighbour but is not unique.
Returning the letter instead of its index, or returning the index inside the count table.
Walking the count table in alphabet order in the second pass. That finds the alphabetically first unique letter, not the first one in the string.

solutions.title: Count each letter on the spot
solutions.idea: For every position, scan the whole string and count how often its letter appears.

solutions.title: Count table, then a second pass
solutions.idea: Count all 26 letters once, then return the first index whose letter has count 1.

followups: The letters arrive as a stream and you must answer after each one. How do you keep the current first unique letter without rescanning?
The string can hold any Unicode character. What changes in the count table?
